newsitem.title: USA: Cargo data networks face cost, Internet pressures.
newsitem.headline: Cargo data networks face cost, Internet pressures.

text.p: Cost pressures and new media competition are likely to force a shakeout among the world's many cargo community data networks, or CCS systems, used by airlines and freight forwarders, a cargo symposium was told.
Airlines' expanding alliances make them better able to negotiate lower fees from national CCS providers, consultant Robert Wagner told Reuters.

Pressure on CCS pricing is already coming from Internet-based services, like E-mail and the shipment tracing systems many carriers put on their home pages, said Malcolm Fowler, systems project manager at British Airways World Cargo.
Fowler told the Journal of Commerce Air Cargo Internet Symposium many CCS providers must adapt or fall by the wayside.

CCS systems may have to merge to meet carriers' demands for lower fees until a handful of global networks remains, said Wagner, a retired Swissair Cargo general manager who advises Swiss information technology company Atraxis.

CCS act as closed electronic networks for EDI messages like airwaybills and shipment status messages between airlines and customers in standardized formats. Large CCS providers include UK-based SITA and Vancouver-based TDNI.
BA uses up to 20 CCS providers and has a budget of over $1 million this year. Fees vary from 20 cents to $1.50 per message, and Fowler said "there is scope for reducing these charges."

Wagner and other speakers said the Internet should be seen as a supplement and not a substitute for CCS or other EDI links which will remain the primary interface for carriers, and their pipeline to other media like Internet and private intranet services.
Internet may never be able to provide all of the functionality of CCSs or intranets, Wagner said

Freight forwarders deal with several airlines who prefer them to use the Internet to access status updates because it costs airlines nothing to dispense it that way. But shippers and freight forwarders do not want to visit each carrier's home page, he added.

Some freight forwarders feel uncomfortable if complete status update information is available to shippers and consignees through unrestricted Internet access, said Unysis Corp executive Larry Mays. Shippers might see their shipment being warehoused while their forwarder builds a consolidation,
To track shipments on the Internet, forwarders or customers must initiate the process, dialing in for each update. CCS may send status updates automatically.
Besides tracking, most integrator and some airline websites handle bookings.
Most symposium speakers were not worried about Internet security or traffic congestion on the Web.

Christopher Shawdon, strategic sales manager for Syntegra, said most Internet cargo messaging forms are small - as opposed to byte intensive graphics - and few users will notice network congestion slowdowns. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017
